      "body": "Slicing a zipped Seq of unknown size from the end overflows the stack:\n\n```js\nSeq([1, 2, 3]).filter(() => true).zip(Seq([4, 5, 6])).slice(-1);\n// RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded\n```\n\n`takeLast(n)`, `zipWith` and `zipAll` do the same.\n\n`sliceFactory` calls `cacheResult()` on a Seq of unknown size before resolving a negative index, then calls itself again. `zipWithFactory` sets `__iterate` on the zipped Seq instead of `__iterateUncached`. `cacheResult()` only does anything when `__iterateUncached` exists, so the size stays unknown and `sliceFactory` recurses forever. With the rename, `Seq#__iterate` uses the cache and `cacheResult()` works.\n\nThis doesn't overlap with #2308, which changes the reverse branch of `__iteratorUncached` in the same factory; the two merge cleanly and the tests pass together.\n\nThe test in `__tests__/zip.ts` fails on `main` and passes with this change.       "body": "`takeLast(0)` returns the whole Seq when its size is unknown:\n\n```js\nSeq([1, 2, 3]).filter(() => true).takeLast(0).toArray(); // [1, 2, 3], expected []\nSeq([1, 2, 3]).takeLast(0).toArray(); // []\n```\n\n#1245 fixed this for known sizes: `takeLast(0)` calls `slice(-0)`, and `resolveIndex` treats `-0` as negative through `isNeg`. But `sliceFactory` decides whether to cache a Seq of unknown size with `begin < 0 || end < 0`, which is false for `-0`, so `resolveBegin(-0, undefined)` comes out as 0 and the slice starts at the beginning.\n\nThis uses `isNeg` for that check (now exported from `TrieUtils`).       "body": "As I grow more comfortable with immutable I've found myself using it all the time - for example just because I needed a stable sort, or to flatten or group structured data, or because it provides a convenient object oriented way of managing common functional transforms using iterators in a way that respects key/value pairs when appropriate.\r\n\r\nWhile I usually want all these things, I don't always want immutability. Thus I am creating Sequins, an implementation of the Immutable.js API backed by es6 native data structures. Its Map and Set types are derived from native (or CoreJS) ones (its List type is not derived from array though). It also includes Indexed, Keyed, and Set sequences.\r\n\r\nBefore I go further I should say that Sequins code is not [yet] at the level of maturity to warrant integration with Immutable. When it is, and I hope to get it there soon (by the time Immutable is ready to release 4.0), I'm happy write the diffs for Immutable. For now I just want to get a start on the discussion of whether integration is reasonable and what problems might be created.\r\n\r\nThe particular integration I'm thinking of is with Immutable's detection of \"data structures\" and keyed collections. Sequins exports a set of sentinel properties almost identical to those of Immutable. It has:\r\n`@@__MUTABLE_ITERABLE__@@`\r\n`@@__MUTABLE_SEQUENCE__@@`\r\n`@@__MUTABLE_KEYED__@@`\r\n`@@__MUTABLE_INDEXED__@@`\r\nMy proposal is for immutable's [Predicates.js](https://github.com/facebook/immutable-js/blob/master/src/Predicates.js) to consider mutable's sentinels as well for the `is*` methods in that file (excluding `isImmutable`) and renaming the old methods to `isImmutable*`. part.text: This matches upstream issue #1992 (fixed by PR #2006). I won't look at the patch — I'll derive the fix myself. part.text:
Fixed. The bug was in `resolveIndex`: when a negative `begin`/`end` was resolved against a collection of unknown size (as after `filter`), `Math.max(0, undefined + index) | 0` coerced `NaN` to `0`, so the slice silently started at index 0 and skipped the cache-first path in `sliceFactory` (src/Operations.js:396) that exists precisely for this NaN case.

Changes:
- src/Operations.js (`CollectionRuntime.resolveIndex`): return `NaN` for a negative index when `size` is unknown.
- src/TrieUtils.js (`resolveIndex`): same fix in the module-level implementation.

`sliceFactory` then caches the filtered seq (computing its size) and re-resolves correctly. Verified: `Range(0,10).filter(x=>true).slice(-2)` → `[8, 9]`, plus negative-end, reverse, takeLast, skip, and known-size cases; full suite passes (44 suites, 684 tests).
